changes.old: ## Зачем изучать N-граммы перед нейронной LM
changes.new: ## Зачем изучать N-граммы перед нейронной LM

### Reading makemore's original count matrix Karpathy's character model counts transitions in a list of 32,033 names. The alphabet has 26 letters plus `.`, giving a $27\times27$ matrix. A row identifies the current character; a column identifies its successor. Each cell prints both the character pair and its count. Darker blue means a larger count, not a larger conditional probability. ![[00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/ngram-makemore-2026-11-03/karpathy-bigram-counts.png|Original makemore character-bigram counts, with pair labels and counts]] *Andrej Karpathy, [makemore Part 1: Bigrams](https://github.com/karpathy/nn-zero-to-hero/blob/73c3fcc741f0ec104ca850b1fb0df90e7e8d4cde/lectures/makemore/makemore_part1_bigrams.ipynb), complete original saved PNG from notebook cell 11, output 0; 884×884 pixels. [MIT license](/licenses/karpathy-nn-zero-to-hero-73c3fcc7-MIT.txt). The source's colors, labels and pixels are unchanged. The dense grid can be opened and enlarged to read individual cells.* The top row starts names; the leftmost column ends them. The source uses the same `.` character for both roles. It adds the boundary character to each name separately, so no transition is counted between consecutive names. At generation time, reaching `.` ends the current name; it does not cause another transition from the boundary row. | Cell | Count | Event counted | |---|---:|---| | `.a` | 4410 | A name starts with a | | `.m` | 2538 | A name starts with m | | `a.` | 6640 | A name ends with a | | `..` | 0 | An empty name | The boundary row sums to 32,033, one first-character event per name. Consequently, its MLE probability for a is $4410/32033\approx0.1377$. The reverse cell `a.` has a different denominator: the a row sums to 33,885, so its MLE probability is $6640/33885\approx0.1960$. Neither count is a probability by itself. Using a column total would instead condition on the following character. The counting cells are retained below. `words` is the original [names.txt](https://github.com/karpathy/makemore/blob/8f79bd0126eaef5eb82d346c9f85ae20ea1c476a/names.txt) split into lines; the 26 letters determine the indices through `stoi`. ```python title="Original makemore cells 7–10 — archival source excerpt" import torch N = torch.zeros((27, 27), dtype=torch.int32) chars = sorted(list(set(''.join(words)))) stoi = {s:i+1 for i,s in enumerate(chars)} stoi['.'] = 0 itos = {i:s for s,i in stoi.items()} for w in words: chs = ['.'] + list(w) + ['.'] for ch1, ch2 in zip(chs, chs[1:]): ix1 = stoi[ch1] ix2 = stoi[ch2] N[ix1, ix2] += 1 ``` *Original source code, unchanged apart from joining notebook cells. The six word-level programs elsewhere in this chapter use the Russian example corpus; this source excerpt uses the names corpus.* The figure is a saved notebook output, not a newly rendered table. Other saved cells reflect later interactive state: cell 12 prints a row of ones, while the figure contains the counts above. Those saved outputs are not treated as a single clean run. The four displayed counts and row totals can be checked by counting the pinned names file independently.

### Row normalization in makemore The source applies add-one to the entire count matrix, then divides each row by its own sum: ```python title="Original makemore cell 23 — archival source excerpt" P = (N+1).float() P /= P.sum(1, keepdims=True) ``` *Andrej Karpathy, [makemore Part 1, cell 23](https://github.com/karpathy/nn-zero-to-hero/blob/73c3fcc741f0ec104ca850b1fb0df90e7e8d4cde/lectures/makemore/makemore_part1_bigrams.ipynb), unchanged code; MIT. The source spelling `keepdims=True` is retained.* Adding one changes every count, including the zero count for `..`. For the first-character row, the denominator becomes $32033+27=32060$; the smoothed probability of a is $4411/32060$. The model now also permits an immediate end marker, with probability $1/32060$, even though no empty name occurred in the data. Before division, `P` has shape $[27,27]$. Summing dimension 1 with the dimension retained gives $[27,1]$: one denominator per history. Broadcasting repeats that denominator across the successor columns. Summing dimension 0 would instead normalize each column and generally leave the row sums unequal to one. A smaller matrix shows the difference without reading 729 cells. Its counts are $[[2,0],[1,3]]$. After adding one, the first row is $[3,1]$ and its denominator is 4; the second row is $[2,4]$ and its denominator is 6. Correct row normalization gives $[3/4,1/4]$ and $[1/3,2/3]$. Column normalization divides by 5 and 5 instead, giving row sums $4/5$ and $6/5$. ```python import torch small_counts = torch.tensor([[2, 0], [1, 3]], dtype=torch.int32) smoothed_counts = (small_counts + 1).double() row_denominators = smoothed_counts.sum(1, keepdim=True) row_probabilities = smoothed_counts / row_denominators torch.testing.assert_close(row_denominators, torch.tensor([[4.], [6.]], dtype=torch.float64)) torch.testing.assert_close(row_probabilities, torch.tensor( [[.75, .25], [1/3, 2/3]], dtype=torch.float64)) torch.testing.assert_close(row_probabilities.sum(1), torch.ones(2, dtype=torch.float64)) column_probabilities = smoothed_counts / smoothed_counts.sum(0, keepdim=True) torch.testing.assert_close(column_probabilities.sum(1), torch.tensor([.8, 1.2], dtype=torch.float64)) ``` ## Backoff и interpolation
